cards.question_text: What are the phases of the incident response process as defined by NIST SP 800-61?
choices: Preparation, Detection & Analysis, Containment/eradication/recovery, Post-incident activity
Plan, Do, Check, Act
Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover
Initiate, Investigate, Isolate, Eradicate, Document
cards.answer: Preparation, Detection & Analysis, Containment/eradication/recovery, Post-incident activity
cards.explanation_correct: NIST SP 800-61 defines four phases: (1) Preparation — building the IR plan, training, tools, contacts before an incident; (2) Detection & Analysis — identifying incidents from alerts/logs and determining scope; (3) Containment, Eradication & Recovery — stopping the spread, removing the threat, restoring systems; (4) Post-incident activity — lessons learned, documentation, improving the process. The NIST lifecycle is cyclic — post-incident feeds back into preparation. This is distinct from the SANS PICERL model (Preparation, Identification, Containment, Eradication, Recovery, Lessons Learned), which maps closely but uses different terminology.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Plan-Do-Check-Act is the Deming cycle (quality management, not IR). Identify-Protect-Detect-Respond-Recover is the NIST CSF (a framework, not the IR process lifecycle). The last option mixes terms that aren't a recognized standard. The common mistake is confusing the NIST CSF functions with the NIST SP 800-61 IR phases — they're related but different documents. IR is specifically about handling incidents after detection; CSF is a broader risk-management framework.

cards.question_text: What is a chain of custody, and why is it critical during incident response and digital forensics?
choices: A documented record of who handled, accessed, and transferred evidence at every step — it preserves evidence integrity and admissibility in legal proceedings
A list of network links connecting the attacker's machines to the victim
A sequence of commands used by the attacker during the intrusion
A backup chain storing copies of evidence on multiple drives
cards.answer: A documented record of who handled, accessed, and transferred evidence at every step — it preserves evidence integrity and admissibility in legal proceedings
cards.explanation_correct: Chain of custody is the chronological documentation showing the custody, control, transfer, analysis, and disposition of evidence. Every person who touches the evidence, when, why, and where must be recorded. Without it, opposing counsel can argue the evidence was tampered with, making it inadmissible in court. It typically uses evidence bags with tamper-evident seals, signed forms, and timestamps. Hashing (e.g., MD5/SHA-256) at collection time proves the data hasn't changed. This matters even for internal incidents because HR/disciplinary actions or law-enforcement referral may require defensible evidence.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Chain of custody is NOT about network topology, attacker command sequences, or backups. It's a legal/forensic concept about evidence handling. The common mistake is thinking digital evidence is self-proving — it isn't. If you can't prove the evidence hasn't been altered from collection to presentation, it's worthless in court. Even imaging a drive without recording who did it and when breaks the chain.

cards.question_text: A security analyst detects a ransomware infection on a file server. Several workstations are also showing encryption activity. The incident is actively spreading. Following NIST IR guidance, what should the response team do FIRST in the containment phase?
choices: Isolate the infected systems from the network (segment/disconnect) to stop lateral spread, while preserving evidence in memory before powering off — then eradicate and recover
Immediately power off all infected machines to stop the encryption
Pay the ransom to decrypt the files as quickly as possible
Send a company-wide email asking employees to not open suspicious attachments
cards.answer: Isolate the infected systems from the network (segment/disconnect) to stop lateral spread, while preserving evidence in memory before powering off — then eradicate and recover
cards.explanation_correct: Short-term containment = isolate infected hosts (disconnect network, VLAN segmentation) to halt lateral movement WITHOUT destroying volatile evidence. Memory contents (running processes, encryption keys, network connections) are lost on power-off, so memory should be captured first. Powering off destroys evidence and can trigger anti-forensic logic in some malware. Eradication (removing malware, patching the entry vector) and recovery (restoring from clean backups) come AFTER containment. Paying the ransom is discouraged (no guarantee, funds crime, may violate OFAC sanctions). Email warnings are part of preparation/communication, not containment.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Powering off is the classic mistake — it destroys volatile evidence (RAM) and some malware is programmed to delete itself or trigger worse behavior on shutdown. Paying the ransom is a last-resort business decision, never a first step, and law enforcement discourages it. Emailing staff doesn't contain an active technical threat. The key concept: contain first (isolate), preserve evidence (memory capture), THEN eradicate and recover. Order matters.

cards.question_text: During a post-incident review (lessons learned), the team discusses a phishing attack that led to credential theft. The root cause was an employee clicking a link despite having completed security awareness training. Which statement best reflects the purpose of this review?
choices: To identify what went wrong and improve processes, controls, and training — not to assign blame to individuals; the goal is systemic improvement so the same incident doesn't recur
To fire the employee who clicked the phishing link as a deterrent to others
To determine how much the incident cost and bill the responsible employee
To document the incident for compliance and then close the case without changing anything
cards.answer: To identify what went wrong and improve processes, controls, and training — not to assign blame to individuals; the goal is systemic improvement so the same incident doesn't recur
cards.explanation_correct: Post-incident activity (lessons learned) is a no-blame, blameless postmortem. The objective is to improve the organization's security posture: Was the phishing filter adequate? Was the training effective or does it need redesign? Should we add MFA? Were detection alerts timely? Blaming individuals creates a culture of fear where people hide incidents, making future breaches worse. The review should produce actionable improvements (new controls, updated playbooks, additional training) and feed back into the Preparation phase of the next cycle. This is why mature teams run blameless retrospectives.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Punitive responses (firing, billing) destroy trust and ensure future incidents go unreported — the worst outcome for security. Documentation-only reviews that change nothing waste the exercise. The common mistake is treating lessons learned as a fault-finding exercise rather than a process-improvement opportunity. A blameless culture surfaces more incidents and more learning; a blame culture hides them.

cards.question_text: A manufacturing company's ICS/SCADA network is hit by a wiper malware that has destroyed historian data and is propagating to engineering workstations. The SOC wants to contain it, but operations cannot tolerate unplanned downtime of the production line. The CISO, plant manager, and legal are on a call. Describe the correct containment approach balancing safety, evidence, and continuity, and explain why simply pulling the plug on the PLCs is wrong.
choices: Use network segmentation/isolation of affected engineering workstations and the historian from the rest of the network while keeping the PLCs running if safe; capture memory and logs from isolated hosts; coordinate containment timing with operations to minimize production impact; do NOT power off PLCs because abrupt shutdowns can cause physical damage or safety hazards in industrial processes, and volatile PLC state may be needed for root-cause analysis
Immediately power off all PLCs and the SCADA network to stop the malware, accepting production loss — safety always means total shutdown
Do nothing and let the malware run its course since the production line must keep running regardless
Reimage all PLCs from backup immediately without preserving any evidence or logs
cards.answer: Use network segmentation/isolation of affected engineering workstations and the historian from the rest of the network while keeping the PLCs running if safe; capture memory and logs from isolated hosts; coordinate containment timing with operations to minimize production impact; do NOT power off PLCs because abrupt shutdowns can cause physical damage or safety hazards in industrial processes, and volatile PLC state may be needed for root-cause analysis
cards.explanation_correct: In OT/ICS environments, containment must account for physical safety and process continuity, not just data integrity. The principle: isolate at the network layer (firewall rules, VLAN isolation) to cut the malware's communication path while allowing the physical process to continue safely. Engineering workstations and the historian (IT-side) can be isolated and forensically imaged. PLCs should NOT be abruptly powered off because (1) industrial processes (chemical reactions, pressure vessels, conveyors) may require controlled shutdown sequences — abrupt power loss can cause explosions, spills, or equipment damage; (2) PLC volatile state and logic may be needed to determine what the attacker changed; (3) some PLCs fail-open or fail-dangerous on power loss. Containment timing is a joint decision (CISO + plant manager + safety officer) following the IR plan. This reflects the NIST SP 800-82 guidance for ICS and the reality that OT incident response differs fundamentally from IT.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Total shutdown is NOT always safer in OT — uncontrolled shutdowns can themselves be the hazard (e.g., a valve that must close in sequence). Doing nothing lets the attacker destroy more. Reimaging without evidence preservation destroys the forensic record and may reintroduce the vulnerability. The common mistake is applying IT incident response instincts (power off, reimage) to OT — where availability and safety often take priority over confidentiality, the inverse of the IT CIA triad. OT IR requires cross-functional coordination and process-aware containment.

cards.question_text: What is the difference between symmetric and asymmetric encryption?
choices: Symmetric uses one shared secret key for both encryption and decryption (fast, good for bulk data); asymmetric uses a key pair — public key encrypts, private key decrypts (slower, good for key exchange and authentication)
Symmetric uses two keys; asymmetric uses one key
Symmetric is only for files; asymmetric is only for network traffic
Symmetric is unbreakable; asymmetric can be broken easily
cards.answer: Symmetric uses one shared secret key for both encryption and decryption (fast, good for bulk data); asymmetric uses a key pair — public key encrypts, private key decrypts (slower, good for key exchange and authentication)
cards.explanation_correct: Symmetric encryption (AES, ChaCha20, 3DES) uses a single shared key — both parties need the same key, so key distribution is the challenge. It's fast and suited for encrypting large amounts of data. Asymmetric encryption (RSA, ECC) uses a mathematically related key pair: the public key can be shared openly and encrypts data; only the private key (kept secret) can decrypt. It's computationally expensive, so in practice systems use asymmetric to exchange a symmetric session key, then use symmetric for the actual data (this is what TLS/HTTPS does). Asymmetric also enables digital signatures (private key signs, public key verifies).
cards.explanation_wrong_common: The number of keys isn't 'two vs one' in the simplistic sense — symmetric needs one key shared by both parties (a distribution problem), asymmetric needs a pair per user. It's not about files vs network. Neither is 'unbreakable' — security depends on key length and algorithm strength; symmetric and asymmetric face different attack models. The common mistake is missing the key-distribution advantage of asymmetric and why hybrid systems (TLS) combine both.

cards.question_text: What is a hash function in cryptography, and how does it differ from encryption?
choices: A hash is a one-way function that maps data of any size to a fixed-length digest — it cannot be reversed (no key, no decryption); encryption is two-way (reversible with a key)
A hash is a type of encryption that uses a secret key to scramble data
A hash and encryption are the same thing with different names
A hash is a two-way function that can be decrypted with the right password
cards.answer: A hash is a one-way function that maps data of any size to a fixed-length digest — it cannot be reversed (no key, no decryption); encryption is two-way (reversible with a key)
cards.explanation_correct: A cryptographic hash (SHA-256, SHA-3, MD5—now broken) takes arbitrary input and produces a fixed-size output (digest). Properties: deterministic (same input → same output), one-way (infeasible to recover input from digest), collision-resistant (hard to find two inputs with the same hash), avalanche effect (tiny input change → completely different hash). Uses: integrity verification (file checksums), password storage (store hash, not password—ideally with salt+pepper via bcrypt/Argon2), digital signatures (sign the hash, not the whole document). Unlike encryption, there's no key and no reversal — you can't 'decrypt' a hash, only compare hashes.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Hashing is NOT encryption — it has no key and is not reversible. Calling it 'encryption with a key' or 'two-way' is fundamentally wrong. The common mistake is conflating hashing with encryption because both 'scramble' data. Encryption is for confidentiality (hide data, recover later); hashing is for integrity/authentication (detect changes, verify identity). Storing passwords encrypted (reversible) instead of hashed is a serious vulnerability — if the key leaks, all passwords are exposed.

cards.question_text: A web application stores user passwords in a database. The developer hashes them with SHA-256. A breach exposes the database, and attackers crack many passwords within hours using rainbow tables. What went wrong, and what is the correct approach?
choices: SHA-256 is a fast general-purpose hash, making it trivial to brute-force/rainbow-table; passwords should be hashed with a slow, salted key-stretching algorithm like bcrypt, scrypt, or Argon2 — the salt defeats rainbow tables and the slowness defeats brute force
SHA-256 is broken and should never be used for anything
The passwords should have been encrypted with AES instead of hashed
The database should not store passwords at all — the app should ask the user each time
cards.answer: SHA-256 is a fast general-purpose hash, making it trivial to brute-force/rainbow-table; passwords should be hashed with a slow, salted key-stretching algorithm like bcrypt, scrypt, or Argon2 — the salt defeats rainbow tables and the slowness defeats brute force
cards.explanation_correct: SHA-256 is designed to be fast (for integrity checks), which is exactly wrong for passwords — attackers can compute billions of SHA-256 hashes/sec on GPUs. Without a salt, identical passwords produce identical hashes, enabling rainbow tables (precomputed hash databases). The fix: (1) Use a password-specific KDF (bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2, PBKDF2) that's deliberately slow and memory-hard, limiting attack speed. (2) Use a unique per-user salt (random, stored alongside the hash) so identical passwords hash differently and rainbow tables are useless. (3) Optionally a pepper (server-side secret) so a DB-only leak still can't crack offline. Argon2id is the current OWASP-recommended choice.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: SHA-256 isn't 'broken' — it's fine for integrity, just wrong for passwords due to speed. Encrypting passwords (AES) is worse — reversible, and a key leak exposes all passwords. 'Don't store anything' breaks authentication (you must verify against something). The common mistake: thinking 'hashed = secure' without considering hash speed and salting. A fast unsalted hash is nearly as bad as plaintext after a breach.

cards.question_text: Two parties want to verify a downloaded file's integrity and authenticity. The publisher provides the file, a SHA-256 hash of the file on their HTTPS website, and a digital signature created with the publisher's private key. Which combination actually proves BOTH integrity AND authenticity (that it came from the publisher, unmodified)?
choices: Verify the digital signature using the publisher's public key (the signature covers the hash of the file) — this proves both integrity (any change invalidates the signature) and authenticity (only the private key holder could have signed it); comparing the SHA-256 hash alone only proves integrity, not authenticity, since anyone can post a hash
Compare the SHA-256 hash only — that proves both integrity and authenticity
Download over HTTPS only — TLS guarantees the file is authentic and unmodified
Check the file size — if it matches the published size, the file is authentic
cards.answer: Verify the digital signature using the publisher's public key (the signature covers the hash of the file) — this proves both integrity (any change invalidates the signature) and authenticity (only the private key holder could have signed it); comparing the SHA-256 hash alone only proves integrity, not authenticity, since anyone can post a hash
cards.explanation_correct: A hash alone proves integrity (file unchanged) IF you trust the source of the hash — but an attacker who replaces the file can also replace the hash on a compromised page. A digital signature ties the hash to a cryptographic identity: the publisher hashes the file and encrypts that hash with their private key. You verify by decrypting the signature with their public key and comparing to your computed hash. Match = the file is unmodified (integrity) AND only someone with the private key could have produced it (authenticity/non-repudiation). HTTPS protects data in transit but not end-state authenticity (a compromised server can serve tampered files over valid TLS). This is why package managers (apt, npm, Sigstore) verify signatures, not just hashes.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Hash ≠ authenticity — it has no identity component. HTTPS ≠ file authenticity — it only secures the channel, not the origin's intent. File size is trivially spoofed. The common mistake is confusing integrity (unchanged) with authenticity (from whom) and non-repudiation (can't deny). Signatures give all three; hashes give only integrity; TLS gives confidentiality + integrity-in-transit but not signed-origin guarantees.

cards.question_text: An application team wants to retire RSA-2048 and move to 'quantum-safe' cryptography. They propose switching all TLS to a post-quantum algorithm they found in a research repo, disabling RSA entirely next week, and storing long-term keys in a plain config file. As a security reviewer, identify the problems with this plan and the correct approach.
choices: Problems: (1) using an unvetted/research-grade PQ algorithm risks implementation flaws and the algorithm may not be standardized; (2) a hard cutover disabling RSA breaks compatibility with existing clients and removes a fallback if the PQ algorithm has a flaw (no crypto agility); (3) storing long-term keys in plaintext config is a key-management failure. Correct approach: adopt NIST-standardized PQ algorithms (e.g., ML-KEM/Kyber, ML-DSA/Dilithium) once finalized, run hybrid mode (classical + PQ together) during transition for agility and fallback, use an HSM or managed KMS for long-term key storage, and phase the migration with compatibility testing
The plan is fine — switching to post-quantum crypto immediately is the safest option and plaintext key storage is acceptable if the server is hardened
Keep RSA-2048 forever because quantum computing is a hoax and post-quantum cryptography doesn't exist
Switch everything to MD5 since it's fast and widely supported
cards.answer: Problems: (1) using an unvetted/research-grade PQ algorithm risks implementation flaws and the algorithm may not be standardized; (2) a hard cutover disabling RSA breaks compatibility with existing clients and removes a fallback if the PQ algorithm has a flaw (no crypto agility); (3) storing long-term keys in plaintext config is a key-management failure. Correct approach: adopt NIST-standardized PQ algorithms (e.g., ML-KEM/Kyber, ML-DSA/Dilithium) once finalized, run hybrid mode (classical + PQ together) during transition for agility and fallback, use an HSM or managed KMS for long-term key storage, and phase the migration with compatibility testing
cards.explanation_correct: This tests several crypto-architecture principles: (1) Standardization — only use vetted, standardized algorithms (NIST's PQC standardization produced FIPS 203/204/205 for ML-KEM/ML-DSA/SLH-DSA in 2024); research repos are for experimentation, not production. (2) Crypto agility — the ability to swap algorithms without redesign; a hard cutover with no fallback is dangerous because if the PQ algorithm is later found flawed (as SIKE was broken in 2022), you have no safety net. Hybrid key exchange (e.g., X25519 + ML-KEM) means an attacker must break BOTH to compromise the session. (3) Key management — long-term keys belong in an HSM/KMS (AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, HashiCorp Vault), never plaintext config files (exposed in backups, version control, memory dumps). Phased migration with testing avoids breaking the ecosystem.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: 'Switch immediately to anything labeled post-quantum' ignores maturity and compatibility — security comes from vetted standards and careful migration, not novelty. Plaintext key storage is never acceptable regardless of host hardening (backups, logs, container escapes). Dismissing quantum risk entirely is also wrong — harvest-now-decrypt-later is a real threat for long-lived secrets. MD5 is broken (collisions trivial). The common mistake is treating crypto as a drop-in upgrade rather than a managed, phased, standards-based lifecycle.

cards.question_text: What is the difference between authentication and authorization?
choices: Authentication verifies WHO you are (proving identity, e.g., password/MFA); authorization determines WHAT you can do (permissions/access rights granted to that identity)
Authentication and authorization are the same thing — both check your password
Authentication grants permissions; authorization checks your password
Authentication is for users; authorization is only for administrators
cards.answer: Authentication verifies WHO you are (proving identity, e.g., password/MFA); authorization determines WHAT you can do (permissions/access rights granted to that identity)
cards.explanation_correct: Authentication (AuthN) answers 'are you who you claim to be?' — validated via factors: something you know (password), have (token/phone), are (biometric). Authorization (AuthZ) answers 'now that we know who you are, what are you allowed to access/do?' — enforced via ACLs, RBAC, ABAC, or policy engines. They're sequential and distinct: you authenticate first, then the system authorizes based on your identity's attributes/roles. A user may authenticate successfully but have zero authorization (a valid account with no permissions). Confusing them leads to broken access control — e.g., authenticating a user but failing to restrict their actions (the #1 OWASP risk: broken access control).
cards.explanation_wrong_common: They are NOT the same and do NOT both check passwords. The reversed definition (authN grants permissions, authZ checks password) is exactly backwards. Authorization isn't admin-only — every authenticated subject (users, services, devices) is subject to authorization. The common mistake: assuming 'logged in = allowed everything.' Authentication establishes identity; authorization is the separate, critical gate on actions. Many breaches occur because authN works but authZ is broken (IDOR, privilege escalation).

cards.question_text: What is the principle of least privilege (PoLP), and how should it be applied to user accounts?
choices: Give users only the minimum access rights needed to perform their job functions — and no more; apply via RBAC/ABAC, time-limited/just-in-time elevation, and periodic access reviews to remove unused permissions
Give every user administrator rights so they can fix their own problems quickly
Give all users the same default access level regardless of role
Give users full access but log everything they do, since monitoring replaces access control
cards.answer: Give users only the minimum access rights needed to perform their job functions — and no more; apply via RBAC/ABAC, time-limited/just-in-time elevation, and periodic access reviews to remove unused permissions
cards.explanation_correct: Least privilege (PoLP / Principle of Least Privilege) is a foundational security principle (from Saltzer & Schroeder, 1975): every subject (user, process, system) should operate using the least set of privileges necessary to complete its task. Implementation: role-based access control (RBAC) or attribute-based (ABAC) to grant role-appropriate rights; just-in-time / time-bound elevation (e.g., PIM tools) so admins get privileged access only for the duration needed; separation of duties (SoD) so no single person can complete a sensitive transaction alone; regular access reviews / recertification to revoke accumulated ('privilege creep') or stale permissions. Default-deny posture: start with no access, grant explicitly. Applies to service accounts and processes too, not just humans.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Universal admin rights, uniform access, and monitoring-as-substitute all violate least privilege. Logging detects misuse but doesn't prevent it — a compromised admin account does damage before logs are reviewed. The common mistake is granting broad access for 'convenience' (privilege creep over time as people change roles). Least privilege must be actively maintained through reviews and automated revocation, not set once. Service accounts are frequently over-privileged and overlooked.

cards.question_text: An organization uses shared admin accounts (one credential for the whole IT team) for convenience. A breach occurs and logs show unauthorized admin actions, but the team cannot determine which person performed them. Which identity practice would have prevented this accountability failure?
choices: Use individual named admin accounts for each administrator (unique credentials per person) plus privileged access management (PAM) that checks out shared resource credentials with per-session attribution — this provides non-repudiation and accountability in logs
Install more cameras in the office to see who was at the keyboard
Require admins to email a manager before each administrative action
Disable all logging since it's not helping identify the person anyway
cards.answer: Use individual named admin accounts for each administrator (unique credentials per person) plus privileged access management (PAM) that checks out shared resource credentials with per-session attribution — this provides non-repudiation and accountability in logs
cards.explanation_correct: Shared credentials destroy accountability/non-repudiation — if five people use one account, logs can't attribute actions to a person, and a compromised shared credential implicates everyone. The fix: (1) Each admin gets a unique named admin account (separate from their daily-use account) so actions are attributed to a person. (2) For unavoidable shared resources, use a PAM/PIM tool (CyberArk, BeyondTrust, Azure PIM) that checks out credentials on demand, ties each session to the requesting user, and rotates the password after checkout. (3) Enforce MFA on all privileged access. This preserves the convenience of shared infrastructure credentials while restoring per-person attribution and non-repudiation.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Cameras and email approvals are administrative workarounds that don't solve digital attribution and don't scale. Disabling logging makes it worse — you lose detection entirely. The common mistake is valuing convenience (one shared password) over accountability, then being unable to investigate an incident. Shared admin accounts also make it impossible to revoke access for a departing employee without disrupting everyone else — another operational risk.

cards.question_text: A company wants to reduce password fatigue and improve security. An analyst proposes single sign-on (SSO) with SAML to one IdP, plus MFA enforced at the IdP. A second analyst worries that if the IdP is compromised, all apps are exposed. Which statement is correct about this SSO design and its risk?
choices: SSO with a trusted IdP and MFA is a strong design that reduces password reuse and centralizes MFA enforcement; the residual risk (IdP compromise = access to all federated apps) is real and must be mitigated by hardening the IdP (MFA, conditional access, monitoring, phishing-resistant MFA like FIDO2/WebAuthn) and maintaining break-glass accounts — the trade-off is generally worth it versus many independent weak passwords
SSO is inherently insecure and should never be used because it creates a single point of failure
SSO eliminates the need for MFA because users only log in once
SSO means each application stores its own copy of the user's password for verification
cards.answer: SSO with a trusted IdP and MFA is a strong design that reduces password reuse and centralizes MFA enforcement; the residual risk (IdP compromise = access to all federated apps) is real and must be mitigated by hardening the IdP (MFA, conditional access, monitoring, phishing-resistant MFA like FIDO2/WebAuthn) and maintaining break-glass accounts — the trade-off is generally worth it versus many independent weak passwords
cards.explanation_correct: SSO (SAML, OIDC) via a central Identity Provider (Okta, Entra ID, Ping) lets users authenticate once and access multiple apps without per-app passwords — reducing password fatigue, reuse, and sprawl, and centralizing MFA, conditional access, and session policies. The valid concern: the IdP becomes a high-value single point of failure (the 'keys to the kingdom'). Mitigations: phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2/WebAuthn security keys — not SMS/PUSH which are phishable), conditional access (device posture, location, risk-based step-up), IdP monitoring/alerting, privileged access management, and break-glass accounts (emergency access, stored securely, monitored) for IdP outage. The trade-off is favorable because the alternative (many independent credentials) is weaker overall — but only if the IdP is rigorously hardened.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: SSO is NOT inherently insecure — used correctly it improves security posture by reducing weak passwords and centralizing controls. SSO does NOT eliminate MFA — MFA at the IdP is the critical control, and SSO actually makes enforcing MFA everywhere easier. SSO does NOT share passwords to apps (that's a password manager's model, not SSO) — apps trust assertions/tokens from the IdP, never seeing the user's password. The common mistake is either dismissing SSO due to SPOF fear without mitigating it, or adopting SSO without hardening the IdP.

cards.question_text: A cloud application uses API keys (long-lived, embedded in client code) to authenticate service-to-service calls. A developer committed a key to a public GitHub repo. The team wants to prevent recurrence and improve the identity model. Recommend a complete remediation covering detection, rotation, and a better service-identity design.
choices: Detection: scan repos/secrets (e.g., GitHub secret scanning, gitleaks) and monitor API key usage for anomalies; Rotation: immediately revoke/rotate the exposed key everywhere it's used (treat all committed keys as compromised); Better design: replace long-lived static API keys with short-lived OAuth2/OIDC tokens issued by an IdP, use workload identity federation (e.g., AWS IAM Roles for Service Accounts, GCP Workload Identity, SPIFFE/SPIRE) so services authenticate via cryptographic identity rather than embedded secrets, enforce least privilege per service, and gate deploys with secret-scanning CI checks to prevent future leaks
Just delete the public repo and the key will be forgotten — attackers only check active repos
Rotate the key once and keep embedding API keys in client code, but add a comment saying 'do not share'
Switch to basic authentication (username/password) instead of API keys, which is more secure
cards.answer: Detection: scan repos/secrets (e.g., GitHub secret scanning, gitleaks) and monitor API key usage for anomalies; Rotation: immediately revoke/rotate the exposed key everywhere it's used (treat all committed keys as compromised); Better design: replace long-lived static API keys with short-lived OAuth2/OIDC tokens issued by an IdP, use workload identity federation (e.g., AWS IAM Roles for Service Accounts, GCP Workload Identity, SPIFFE/SPIRE) so services authenticate via cryptographic identity rather than embedded secrets, enforce least privilege per service, and gate deploys with secret-scanning CI checks to prevent future leaks
cards.explanation_correct: This is a real-world cloud identity failure pattern. (1) Detection: automated secret scanning (GitHub Advanced Security, gitleaks, truffleHog) catches committed secrets; API usage monitoring/anomaly detection catches active abuse. (2) Rotation: any committed secret must be treated as compromised and revoked immediately — attackers scrape git history, so deletion alone is ineffective. Rotate across all environments and update consumers. (3) Better design: long-lived embedded keys are the anti-pattern. Workload identity federation lets a service prove its identity cryptographically (e.g., a Kubernetes service account token exchanged for cloud credentials via OIDC federation) — no static secrets to leak, automatic rotation, least-privilege per workload. SPIFFE/SPIRE provides a general SVID framework. Short-lived OAuth2/OIDC tokens limit blast radius. CI secret-scanning gates prevent recurrence. This aligns with zero-trust and cloud-native identity best practices.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Deleting the repo doesn't help — git is distributed and attackers/scrapers already cached it; secrets in history persist. 'Rotate once and keep the pattern' leaves the root cause (static embedded secrets) intact. Basic auth (username/password) is weaker than API keys and also a static secret — it's a downgrade. The common mistake is treating the leak as a one-time incident rather than a systemic identity-model flaw. The fix is eliminating static secrets via workload identity, not just rotating them.

cards.question_text: What is a firewall, and what is the difference between a stateful inspection firewall and a stateless (packet-filtering) firewall?
choices: A firewall is a network security device/ software that filters traffic based on rules. A stateless firewall filters each packet independently against static rules (fast but context-blind); a stateful firewall tracks the state of connections (established, related) and allows return traffic for approved sessions — more secure, understands context
A firewall is an antivirus program that scans files for malware
A firewall encrypts all network traffic to keep it confidential
A stateful firewall is slower and less secure than a stateless one
cards.answer: A firewall is a network security device/ software that filters traffic based on rules. A stateless firewall filters each packet independently against static rules (fast but context-blind); a stateful firewall tracks the state of connections (established, related) and allows return traffic for approved sessions — more secure, understands context
cards.explanation_correct: A firewall enforces an access control policy between network segments (e.g., internet ↔ DMZ ↔ internal) by permitting/denying traffic per rules. Stateless (packet-filtering) firewalls examine each packet in isolation — source/dest IP, port, protocol — without memory of prior packets. Fast but can't distinguish a legitimate response from a spoofed one. Stateful firewalls maintain a state table of active connections; they know a packet is part of an established session and allow return traffic automatically (the 'established/related' rule), while blocking unsolicited inbound traffic. Next-gen firewalls (NGFW) add deep packet inspection, app-awareness, and IPS. Stateful is the modern baseline; stateless survives in simple routers/ACLs.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: A firewall is NOT antivirus (different layer — network vs file). It does NOT encrypt traffic (that's VPN/TLS). Stateful is MORE secure than stateless, not less — the 'slower' perception is outdated; modern stateful inspection is hardware-accelerated. The common mistake is thinking packet filtering alone is sufficient — stateless firewalls can't properly handle protocols that use dynamic ports (FTP, SIP) because they can't relate the data channel to the control session. State tracking solves this.

cards.question_text: What is a DMZ (demilitarized zone) in network architecture, and what is its purpose?
choices: A perimeter network segment that hosts public-facing services (web, email, DNS) so that if those services are compromised, the attacker is contained in the DMZ and doesn't have direct access to the internal/trusted network
A zone where all network traffic is encrypted end-to-end
A backup network used only when the main network fails
A wireless network reserved for guest access with no security controls
cards.answer: A perimeter network segment that hosts public-facing services (web, email, DNS) so that if those services are compromised, the attacker is contained in the DMZ and doesn't have direct access to the internal/trusted network
cards.explanation_correct: A DMZ is a buffered subnet between the untrusted internet and the trusted internal LAN, enforced by firewalls (often two: external firewall internet↔DMZ, internal firewall DMZ↔internal). Public-facing servers (web, mail, external DNS) live in the DMZ because they must accept internet connections and are therefore higher-risk. If an attacker compromises a DMZ host, they still face the internal firewall to reach corporate resources — segmentation buys defense-in-depth. Rules: DMZ hosts should NOT initiate connections inbound to the internal net; internal users can access DMZ; internet can access only specific DMZ ports. This is a core defense-in-depth / segmentation pattern; modern equivalents use cloud security groups and zero-trust microsegmentation.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: DMZ is not an encryption zone, a backup network, or an open guest Wi-Fi. The guest network is separate (and should still be isolated from internal). The common mistake is placing internal-only services in the DMZ (unnecessary exposure) or, worse, allowing DMZ hosts to talk freely to the internal network (defeats the containment purpose). The DMZ's value is containment via segmentation — if compromised services have a clear path inward, the DMZ is theater.

cards.question_text: A company deploys a traditional network-based IDS (NIDS) at the internet edge. It sees encrypted TLS traffic entering the network and can only inspect packet headers, not payload. Many modern attacks hide in encrypted channels. Which approach best addresses this blind spot without breaking encryption for users?
choices: Deploy TLS inspection (SSL/TLS decryption) at a forward proxy or next-gen firewall with a trusted root CA deployed to clients — the appliance decrypts, inspects for threats, then re-encrypts onward; combined with EDR for endpoint visibility. Consider privacy/compliance (inspect only where justified, exclude banking/health sites via bypass rules)
Block all encrypted traffic so everything is plaintext and inspectable
Disable TLS on the company website to let the IDS see traffic
Rely solely on the IDS headers since encrypted attacks are rare
cards.answer: Deploy TLS inspection (SSL/TLS decryption) at a forward proxy or next-gen firewall with a trusted root CA deployed to clients — the appliance decrypts, inspects for threats, then re-encrypts onward; combined with EDR for endpoint visibility. Consider privacy/compliance (inspect only where justified, exclude banking/health sites via bypass rules)
cards.explanation_correct: With ~80%+ of web traffic encrypted, a NIDS that only sees headers misses payloads (malware C2, exfiltration, exploits). TLS inspection (aka SSL decryption) uses a forward proxy/NGFW that holds a trusted CA certificate installed on endpoints; it performs a man-in-the-middle: decrypts inbound TLS, runs IPS/malware inspection, then re-encrypts to the destination. Critical considerations: (1) Deploy a trusted root CA to managed devices. (2) Privacy/compliance — bypass categories like banking/health/government to avoid violating regulations or employee privacy; log per policy. (3) Some apps use certificate pinning (mobile banking) and will fail — exclude them. (4) Supplement with EDR (endpoint detection) which sees decrypted payload at the endpoint, covering blind spots where inspection isn't feasible. TLS inspection is the standard enterprise solution but must be deployed with legal/HR awareness.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Blocking all encrypted traffic or disabling TLS destroys confidentiality and breaks the modern web (and your own site's security) — unacceptable. 'Encrypted attacks are rare' is false — attackers deliberately use TLS to evade IDS. The common mistake is accepting the encrypted blind spot as unfixable; TLS inspection is mature and widely deployed. The second mistake is inspecting everything without privacy controls, which creates legal/HR liability — selective bypass is part of a responsible deployment.

cards.question_text: A network engineer is configuring a VPN for remote workers. They propose using PPTP because it's built into old Windows clients and 'just works.' As a security reviewer, what do you advise, and what VPN protocol should be used instead?
choices: Reject PPTP — it uses weak MS-CHAPv2 authentication and broken encryption (MPPE), exploitable in minutes; use IPsec (strong, standardized, native support) or WireGuard (modern, fast, simple, strong crypto) or TLS-based VPN (OpenVPN) instead, with MFA enforced on VPN access
PPTP is fine for internal use since it's behind a firewall
Use L2TP without encryption since it's widely supported
VPN protocols don't matter as long as users have strong passwords
cards.answer: Reject PPTP — it uses weak MS-CHAPv2 authentication and broken encryption (MPPE), exploitable in minutes; use IPsec (strong, standardized, native support) or WireGuard (modern, fast, simple, strong crypto) or TLS-based VPN (OpenVPN) instead, with MFA enforced on VPN access
cards.explanation_correct: PPTP is obsolete and insecure: MS-CHAPv2 is crackable in minutes (Moxie Marlinspike demonstrated this), and MPPE encryption uses weak RC4 keys derived from the weak auth. It should never be used in production, even 'internally' (a compromised VPN tunnel reaches the internal network). Recommended: (1) IPsec/IKEv2 — the enterprise standard, strong, natively supported on most OSes, good mobile reconnection. (2) WireGuard — modern, minimal attack surface, state-of-the-art crypto (ChaCha20, Curve25519), fast, but newer. (3) OpenVPN (TLS-based) — mature, widely supported, configurable. Regardless of protocol, enforce MFA on VPN (it's an internet-exposed auth point) and apply least privilege (split-tunnel only needed routes, not full corporate network by default).
cards.explanation_wrong_common: PPTP isn't saved by being 'behind a firewall' — the VPN itself is internet-facing for authentication, and weak crypto means the tunnel can be broken. L2TP without encryption is just a tunneling protocol with no confidentiality — useless alone (L2TP/IPsec pairs it). 'Protocols don't matter' is wrong — protocol choice determines the cryptographic strength of the tunnel. The common mistake is prioritizing convenience/legacy compatibility over security; PPTP's 'just works' quality is precisely because it's old and weak.

cards.question_text: An enterprise is moving from a traditional perimeter model (firewall + DMZ, trust inside) to Zero Trust. A junior architect proposes 'just remove the firewall and put MFA on everything.' Explain why this is insufficient and describe the core Zero Trust principles and the network/identity controls actually required.
choices: Removing the firewall is not Zero Trust — ZT doesn't remove controls, it removes implicit trust. Core principles: (1) verify explicitly per-request (identity + device posture + context), never trust based on network location; (2) least-privilege access via policy (RBAC/ABAC, JIT elevation); (3) assume breach — microsegmentation, continuous monitoring, encrypt all traffic (even internal), inspect and log all access. Required controls: strong identity (IdP + phishing-resistant MFA), device health/compliance attestation (MDM/EDR), policy engine (ZTNA, service mesh), microsegmentation (per-workload firewalls), continuous telemetry/analytics, and identity-aware proxies replacing flat network trust. Firewalls/segmentation still exist but become granular and policy-driven, not a single trusted/untrusted boundary
Zero Trust means trusting nothing and therefore having no network at all — disconnect everything
Zero Trust is just MFA plus VPN, which is what the company already has
Zero Trust requires buying one specific vendor's product and it will handle everything automatically
cards.answer: Removing the firewall is not Zero Trust — ZT doesn't remove controls, it removes implicit trust. Core principles: (1) verify explicitly per-request (identity + device posture + context), never trust based on network location; (2) least-privilege access via policy (RBAC/ABAC, JIT elevation); (3) assume breach — microsegmentation, continuous monitoring, encrypt all traffic (even internal), inspect and log all access. Required controls: strong identity (IdP + phishing-resistant MFA), device health/compliance attestation (MDM/EDR), policy engine (ZTNA, service mesh), microsegmentation (per-workload firewalls), continuous telemetry/analytics, and identity-aware proxies replacing flat network trust. Firewalls/segmentation still exist but become granular and policy-driven, not a single trusted/untrusted boundary
cards.explanation_correct: Zero Trust (NIST SP 800-207) is a paradigm shift: never trust, always verify — based on identity and context, not network location. The 'trust the inside' assumption of the castle-and-moat model fails because lateral movement after a breach has no internal barriers. ZT principles: (1) Verify explicitly — every access request is authenticated and authorized against identity + device posture + behavioral/context signals, per-request, not per-session. (2) Least-privilege access — JIT, JEA, RBAC/ABAC, minimize standing privilege. (3) Assume breach — microsegmentation (per-workload or per-segment firewalls), encrypt all traffic (mTLS internally), continuous monitoring and analytics, and inspect/log all access. Controls: an IdP with phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2), device compliance via MDM/EDR, a policy decision point (ZTNA, service mesh like Istio, or Cloudflare Access), microsegmentation (host-based firewalls, NSGs), and SIEM/analytics for continuous trust evaluation. Critically, firewalls and segmentation are NOT removed — they're made granular and dynamic, replacing the binary trusted/untrusted boundary with per-request policy. 'Remove the firewall + MFA' is a caricature that loses segmentation while adding only one control.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Zero Trust is NOT 'no network' or 'disconnect everything' — it's a more rigorous, identity-driven network model, not abolition. It's NOT 'MFA + VPN' — VPN extends the trusted perimeter (the opposite of ZT); ZTNA replaces VPN with per-app, identity-aware access without network-level trust. It's NOT a single product — ZT is an architecture spanning identity, device, network, and monitoring; vendors sell pieces, not 'Zero Trust in a box.' The common mistakes: (a) treating ZT as a product purchase rather than an architecture; (b) removing perimeter controls without replacing them with microsegmentation (you end up LESS secure); (c) keeping flat internal networks and just adding MFA at the gate — that's not ZT, that's castle-and-moat with a stronger door. Real ZT requires verifying every request, segmenting every workload, and assuming the adversary is already inside.
